results.summary_before: This design converts ASCII characters to ITU Morse code, streaming the elements on a key line and generating a PWM sidetone for the TT Audio Pmod. It also displays status bits on the 7-segment display, with options for speed selection, tone selection, and auto-repeat. The chip handles all Morse timing and provides a handshake protocol so a host can stream text without dropping characters. It is tested with a cocotb testbench and can be driven from a microcontroller using the ttboard SDK.

results.summary_before: This tile contains four instances of a 1.8 V rail-to-rail input and output operational amplifier whose inputs are shared and whose outputs are multiplexed onto a single analog pin. An instance is selected with two digital select pins and enabled with a separate enable pin. The documentation notes that compensation is not very good, so the amplifier may not be unity-gain stable in practice, and it is optimized for roughly 10 pF of load capacitance. Testing requires external analog signal sources and a load on the selected output, and the documentation is otherwise brief.

results.summary_before: This design implements a compact 16-bit Galois LFSR-based pseudo-random number generator with deterministic self-seeding, automatic polynomial switching, repetition detection, and cooldown control. It uses three internally selectable polynomials and generates an 8-bit output from the lower bits of the LFSR state. The PRNG is enabled via an input pin and seeded externally through 7 bits, with an 8-bit repetition monitor that triggers polynomial switching and reseeding when consecutive outputs repeat. The design is verified with a cocotb testbench covering reset, seeding, LFSR operation, and adaptive behavior.

results.summary_before: This project is a multi-pattern LED sequencer that drives eight LEDs with thirty-one selectable patterns plus a demo mode that cycles through all of them. Pattern selection is set by five input pins, and two further pins choose between 1 Hz, 2 Hz, 5 Hz and 50 Hz clock rates derived from the 10 MHz input by an internal divider. Patterns are generated using counters, feedback loops and an LFSR for pseudo-random sequences, and the design is split into a PLL/divider module and the main MPLS module. Testing is done through Icarus Verilog testbenches, with a full-pattern simulation and a longer PLL simulation that can produce very large VCD files.
